sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does each heading name what its section holds?** No. The right-hand heading "If something goes wrong" (about x 660–925, y 148–172) promises help with any problem. The three numbered steps below it (y 190–380) are only a way to report one afterwards: write down the crossing details, describe the problem, then leave the note at the quay office or post it. Someone who has just missed the last boat, lost their ticket, or cannot get a pram on board will scan for help, land on this heading, and find a complaint form. The heading also doesn't say what happens after you report, and the last step sends the reader to "the address on the noticeboard" rather than giving the address. That turns the "help" into a third errand. WCAG 2.4.6 (Headings and Labels) says headings should describe the topic or purpose of their section. This heading names a situation, not what the section does. Fix: name what the section does, for example "Report a problem with your crossing". If the sheet is meant to help when things go wrong, add the immediate action first (ask the crew, or call the quay office) before the reporting steps. Print the address on the sheet. Mark: defect (it sends a passenger in trouble to the wrong place). Weight: minor, because the sheet still works for its main jobs. It would be major if this sheet is where passengers turn for help during a disruption.

**What's working.**
- **Clear purpose:** The piece says what it is in one look. The title "Help for ferry passengers" and two task-named columns ("Before you board" and a problem column) make the purpose clear in a sentence, with nothing decorative in the way. Every element on the page carries information.
- **Bullets versus numbers:** Bullets hold the loose tips and numbers hold the ordered steps. The difference tells the reader which part is a sequence, and each kind is styled the same wherever it appears.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (each heading names what its section holds).

sections.report:
**Walk (working notes)**

The image is 1280×800, about one screen, so I worked from the whole image and made no crops.

First read: the eye lands on "Help for ferry passengers" at the top left. It moves to the two bold headings, then into the left column. The page reads as a plain, calm help sheet for ferry passengers. Assumed job: a printed or on-screen notice that passengers scan for practical rules and what to do if something goes wrong.

What matters first:
- One element stands clearly above the rest: **yes**. The title is about 40 px bold, roughly twice the headings.
- Each text level can be told from the next, with no near-equal sizes: **yes**. There are three levels: title (about 40 px), headings (about 22 px bold), and body (about 18 px regular). Heading and body are close in size, but the weight difference makes them separate at a glance.
- Headings differ from text in more than size: **yes**. They are bold and slightly darker.

No line came out `no` or `unsure`, so I opened no entries.

---

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The title clearly leads.** "Help for ferry passengers" (top left, about y 60–110) is about twice the size of the headings and heavy. A passenger knows at once what the sheet is and where to start.
- **Weight does the work between headings and body.** "Before you board" and "If something goes wrong" (y ≈ 160) are only a little larger than the body text. Their bold weight still marks them as headings, so the page reads as two clear sections without a crowded size scale. This is the "bolder, not bigger" approach from Wathan and Schoger, *Refactoring UI*.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do lines of text in neighboring columns sit on the same baselines? No.** The two columns line up through the headings (y≈159) and the first two lines (y≈203, 230). After that they drift apart because each item adds about 14 px of space on a 27 px line pitch, and the left items run three lines while the right ones run two. Right item 2 starts at y≈271, between the left column's lines at 257 and 298. Right item 3 sits at y≈339/366, between the left lines at 325/352/393. Across the 70 px gutter the rows stop matching from the second item down, so the two columns look set separately rather than on one grid. A reader moving between columns has no shared lines to follow. Source: Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*, "Construction of the grid". Fix: make the space between items a whole line (27 px) or half a line, so every line in both columns falls on the same baselines. Convention. Weight: minor.
2. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip? No.** The left column runs to y≈550, but the right column stops at y≈380. That leaves an empty block of about 490×420 px in the lower right, joined to an empty band across the whole page from y≈560 to 800, about 30% of the frame. All the weight sits in the top left, so the page looks unfinished, as if content is missing, rather than calm. Source: Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance". If this is a scrolling web page, the empty bottom is just viewport and is not a problem. If it is a fixed frame (a screen, slide or posted notice), fix it in one of two ways: scale the type and spacing up so the content fills the frame, or give the short right column something that balances the left (for example, set the quay office contact apart below the steps). Taste. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The two columns follow the order a passenger needs: "Before you board" first, then "If something goes wrong". Each column has a single left edge (x≈90 and x≈660) shared with the title, so the page reads as a clear two-part grid with an obvious path from the title down the left and then the right.
- The spacing shows the groups clearly. The gap from the title to the section headings (~45 px) is bigger than the gap from each heading to its list (~20 px), which is bigger than the gap between items (~14 px extra). Each heading sits with its own list, and each item reads as a separate unit.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** I can't tell whether the empty bottom band is part of a fixed frame or just leftover viewport on a web page, and that decides whether finding 2 matters. Bash was blocked, so I couldn't run the crop script. I judged from the whole image, which is about one screen.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (lines align across columns; weight balances)

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the left edge of each text block stay crisp, with wrapped list lines under the first word and opening quotation marks hung outside?** No.
   - **Where:** In the left column, each bullet sits at x≈90 and its text starts at x≈115, but the wrapped lines go back to x≈90, under the bullet. This happens on lines like "because winter sailings…", "the machine is slow…" and "boarded and lock them…". The numbered list on the right does the same: wrapped lines start at x≈660, under "1." / "2." / "3.", not under the first word at x≈681.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** Bullets and numbers do not stand out in a margin of their own, so each item looks like a small paragraph with a mark stuck on its first line. The wide gap after each bullet makes the first line look indented and the rest outdented. The step numbers 1–3 also sink into the text. A passenger scanning "If something goes wrong" for the next step has to find where it starts, when the numbers should catch the eye down the left edge.
   - **Why:** Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, 4.4.2, p. 71, says to clarify lists through spatial positioning and to hang the numbers in the margin. The narrower rule, that wrapped lines align with the first word, has no confirmed source, so that part is common sense.
   - **Fix:** Use a hanging indent so every wrapped line aligns with the item's first word and the bullets and numbers sit alone in the margin. On the web, real `ul`/`ol` markers with `list-style-position: outside` do this. Also close the bullet-to-text gap to about one word space plus a little.
   - **Kind:** Convention. **Weight:** Major, because these are the two lists that carry all of the piece's content, and step order matters for the "goes wrong" steps.
2. **Do paragraphs and columns break cleanly, with no lone short word on a last line and no heading at the foot of a column?** No.
   - **Where:** Bullet 4 in the left column ends with "clear." alone on its last line (x≈90, y≈542). Bullet 3's "lower deck." (y≈447) is nearly as short.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** A lone word leaves a hole at the bottom of the item and is the last thing the eye meets in the column, so it reads as a leftover rather than the end of a sentence.
   - **Why:** Bringhurst, 2.4.2, says a paragraph should not end with one short word alone on its last line.
   - **Fix:** Rewrap so at least two words share the last line, by editing the sentence, adding a non-breaking space before the last word, or using `text-wrap: pretty`. Fixing finding 1 changes the measure and may solve this on its own.
   - **Kind:** Convention. **Weight:** Minor.

**What's working.**
- **Comfortable reading setting:** The body text is a plain sans at a comfortable size, about 18–19 px. It is near-black on white, with lines of about 55–60 characters in each column and generous, even line spacing. Long instructions read without effort, which suits passengers reading on the move.
- **Clear sizes and weights:** There are three sizes, each with a plain job: a bold title at about 40 px, bold column headings at about 22 px, and regular body text. Nothing sits a step or two from another size, and the headings differ from the body by weight as well as size.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 28 yes, 2 no (paragraphs and columns break cleanly; left edge crisp with hanging bullets), 0 unsure

Bash was refused, so I did not run the crop script and judged from the whole image, which is about one screen.

**First read.** The eye lands on the bold title "Help for ferry passengers", then drops to the two column heads and their lists. It reads as a plain, calm help page for ferry passengers. It is grayscale only: near-black text on white, with no hue anywhere.

**Job (assumed).** A help page that ferry passengers read to prepare for a crossing or to report a problem.

**Walk (Color).**
- Small palette: yes. It uses one near-black or dark gray for text on a white background.
- Saturated color kept to a small share: yes. There is none.
- Clear range of light and dark: yes. The dark text on white holds full contrast, and the structure comes from weight and size, so it survives in grayscale.
- Warm forward, cool back: yes. There are no hues.
- Matching colors look the same everywhere: yes. Headings and body text use the same ink throughout.
- No vibrating edges: yes. There are no neighbouring strong colors.
- Status colors used only for their usual meaning: yes. There are none.
- Meaning not carried by color alone: yes. Nothing is color-coded. Bullets and numbers carry the structure.
- Dark theme background: yes. It is a light page, so this line doesn't come into play.

No line came out `no` or `unsure`, so there was nothing to open in the reference entries.

---

**Section.** Color: applies. The page is grayscale only.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- Every text element is dark ink on white: the title at about y 65–105, the column heads at y 150–170, and the body text in both columns. That gives the strongest contrast the page can have. Passengers reading on a phone outdoors or in a dim shelter lose nothing to faint gray text.
- The page doesn't use color to mark structure. The levels come from size and weight, and the lists come from bullets and numbers. So nothing depends on seeing color, and if a single accent color is added later (for example, for the quay office address), it has room to stand out.

**Checklist.** `Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure`
